title: Pipelines, stages and artifacts
summary: How a pipeline is shaped, what it hands from step to step, and where it deploys.

steps.title: Stages and fail-fast
body: A pipeline is a sequence of **stages**; each stage holds one or more **jobs**, each job is a list of **steps** (commands).
Stages run **in order** and the pipeline **fails fast**: when a stage fails, later stages are *skipped*. There is no point
packaging code that does not compile. Put the quickest, most likely-to-fail checks first so feedback arrives fast.

steps.prompt: The `test` stage fails. What does the run summary show for `deploy`?
steps.explain: After the first failure every later stage is skipped, not failed: it never ran.

steps.title: Artifacts: build once, deploy many
body: An **artifact** is the output of a job that later jobs (or people) need: a zipped publish folder, a NuGet package, a Docker image,
The golden rule: **build once, promote the same artifact**. If you rebuild for production you are shipping something that was never tested.
(same bytes everywhere, named by version and commit)
Name artifacts so you can trace them back: app, version, and the short commit SHA.

steps.prompt: Staging passed, so the release job runs `dotnet publish` again and deploys the new output to production. What is the problem?
options: Production gets bytes that were never tested; a dependency or tool may have changed between builds
Publishing twice is slower but otherwise identical
`dotnet publish` cannot run in a release job
steps.explain: Rebuilds can pick up a new package version, a different SDK or a changed environment variable. Promote the artifact you tested.

steps.title: Environments
body: An **environment** is a place the app runs: `dev`, `staging`, `production`. Each has its own configuration, secrets and,
usually, its own protection rules (who may deploy, required approvals, wait timers).
Changes are **promoted** through environments in a fixed order. Configuration differs per environment; the artifact does not.

steps.prompt: Match each environment feature to the problem it solves.
pairs: staging cannot read the production database password
a pause to watch the previous environment before continuing

steps.prompt: Complete the artifact name: app `api`, version `1.4.0`, commit `3f2a9c1e88...`.
steps.explain: `latest` and branch names change meaning over time. A version plus a short SHA always points at exactly one build.

steps.title: A fail-fast runner
prompt: Write `List<string> RunPipeline(List<(string Stage, bool Passes)> stages)` that returns one log line per stage:
- `"deploy: skipped"` for every stage after a failure.
Example: `[(build, true), (test, false), (deploy, true)]` → `build: ok`, `test: FAILED`, `deploy: skipped`.
starter: List<string> RunPipeline(List<(string Stage, bool Passes)> stages)
solution: List<string> RunPipeline(List<(string Stage, bool Passes)> stages)
hints: Keep a `bool failed` flag outside the loop.
Once `failed` is true, every later stage is logged as skipped, whether or not it would pass.
template: Dojo.Eq("all green", new List<string> { "build: ok", "test: ok" }, RunPipeline(new() { ("build", true), ("test", true) }));
Dojo.Eq("failure skips the rest", new List<string> { "build: ok", "test: FAILED", "package: skipped", "deploy: skipped" },
Dojo.Eq("first stage fails", new List<string> { "build: FAILED", "test: skipped" }, RunPipeline(new() { ("build", false), ("test", false) }));
